tldr.label: Key takeaways
tldr.lead: A Cornell notes template is a page split into three zones: a narrow cue column on the left, a wide notes column on the right, and a summary strip across the bottom. You can copy the version below into Google Docs, Notion, Word or GoodNotes in under five minutes.
bullets: The method comes from Walter Pauk, who directed the Reading and Study Center at Cornell University and published it in How to Study in College (first edition 1962).
The classic layout on US Letter paper is a 2.5-inch cue column, a 6-inch notes column and a 2-inch summary at the bottom.
The 5 Rs (Record, Reduce, Recite, Reflect, Review) matter more than the lines. The cue column only works if you fill it after the lecture and then quiz yourself with it.
If writing while listening overloads you, as it often does with ADHD, let a transcript handle the recording step and spend your energy on the cues and the summary.

intro: A Cornell notes template is a note-taking page divided into three zones: a cue column for questions and keywords, a notes column for what was said in the lecture, and a summary box at the bottom where you condense the page into a few sentences. Walter Pauk designed the system at Cornell University in the 1950s and published it in How to Study in College, which is still in print. The layout is simple, but most students use only half of it. They fill the notes column and leave the cue column empty, which removes the self-testing step that makes the method work. This guide gives you the template itself, a copy-paste version for Google Docs, Notion, Microsoft Word and GoodNotes, a fully filled example from a psychology lecture, and a version adapted for students with ADHD who struggle to write and listen at the same time.

sections.body:
Cornell notes are a structured note-taking format that separates **capturing** information from **processing** it. During the lecture you write only in the notes column. After the lecture you go back, pull out questions and keywords into the cue column, and write a short summary at the bottom. The page becomes a self-test: cover the notes column, read the cues, and try to answer them from memory.

The system was created by **Walter Pauk**, an education professor who ran the Reading and Study Center at Cornell University. He described it in **How to Study in College**, first published in 1962 and revised through more than ten editions. Cornell's Learning Strategies Center still publishes a guide to it for students today.

The reason Cornell notes have outlived most study fads is that they build retrieval practice into the page itself. Rereading notes feels productive but tests nothing. Answering your own cue questions with the notes covered is active recall, the same technique behind flashcards, and it is one of the most consistently supported study strategies in learning research.

sections.h2: What does a Cornell notes template look like?
sections.body: A Cornell notes template is one page with two columns and a footer. On US Letter paper (8.5 x 11 inches), Pauk's original measurements are a **2.5-inch cue column** on the left, a **6-inch notes column** on the right, and a **2-inch summary** across the bottom. On A4 paper, the equivalent is roughly 6 cm, 15 cm and 5 cm. The exact numbers matter less than the ratio: about 30% cues, 70% notes. Here is the layout as a template you can mirror:

rows: Header: course, lecture title, date
Header: course, lecture title, date
Filled AFTER class: questions, keywords, names, formulas you want to be quizzed on
Filled DURING class: main ideas, facts, definitions, examples, diagrams; short phrases, not full sentences
One cue per idea, lined up next to the note it points to
Leave a blank line between ideas so cues can sit beside them
Summary (full width, 2 in, bottom)
3-4 sentences in your own words: what this page is about and why it matters

callout.label: Why the cue column is on the left
callout.body: Pauk put the cues on the left so you can fold or cover the notes column and see only the questions. If you build the template digitally, keep that property: the cues must be readable while the notes are hidden.

sections.h2: What are the 5 Rs of Cornell notes?
sections.body: The 5 Rs of Cornell notes are the five steps Pauk prescribed for using the page: Record, Reduce, Recite, Reflect and Review. The template is only the container. The 5 Rs are the method.

steps.detail: During the lecture, write the main ideas and supporting facts in the notes column. Use abbreviations and short phrases. Skip anything you can look up later in the slides.
As soon as possible after the lecture, ideally the same day, read your notes and condense each idea into a question or keyword in the cue column. Then write the summary at the bottom.
Cover the notes column. Read each cue and answer it out loud in your own words. Uncover to check. Mark every cue you missed.
Ask how this lecture connects to earlier ones, to the reading, or to an exam question. Write those links in the margin or the summary.
Spend about ten minutes a week reciting from the cue columns of older pages. Focus on the cues you marked as missed.

sections.h2: Cornell notes template you can copy and paste
sections.body: This is a plain-text Cornell notes template in Markdown. Copy it into Notion, Obsidian, Google Docs (turn on **Tools > Preferences > Enable Markdown**, then right-click and choose **Paste from Markdown**), or any notes app. Plain Markdown has no side-by-side columns, so the cues sit in their own section above the notes. Each cue is numbered to match a note, which keeps the self-test working.

callout.label: Copy-paste Cornell template (Markdown)
callout.body:
# [Course] | [Lecture title] | [Date]

## Cues (fill after class)

Q1: [Question the first idea answers]

Q2: [Keyword, name or formula to remember]

Q3: [Question an exam could ask]

## Notes (fill during class)

N1: [Main idea, short phrases]

N2: [Fact, definition or example]

N3: [Diagram description, link to slide]

## Summary (3-4 sentences, your own words)

[What this lecture was about and why it matters]

## Missed cues to review

[Q numbers you could not answer]

sections.h2: How do you make a Cornell notes template in Google Docs, Notion, Word or GoodNotes?
sections.body: You can build a reusable Cornell notes template in any of these apps in about five minutes. Build it once, then duplicate it for every lecture.

subsections.body: Go to **Insert > Table** and create a 2 x 3 table. Put the course and date in the top row, cues and notes in the middle row, and merge the bottom row (select both cells, right-click, **Merge cells**) for the summary. Open **Format > Table > Table properties** and set the left column to about a third of the right column, for example 2 and 4.5 inches with default margins. Name the file "Cornell master" and use **File > Make a copy** before each lecture.

Type **/2 columns** to create a side-by-side block, then drag the divider until the left column is roughly 30% wide. Put a heading "Cues" on the left and "Notes" on the right, and add a callout block below both columns for the summary. To reuse it, create a database called "Lectures", click the arrow next to **New**, choose **New template**, and paste the layout inside. Every new lecture page will start with the Cornell layout.

Use **Insert > Table** for a 2 x 3 grid, merge the bottom row with **Layout > Merge Cells**, and set column widths under **Layout > Properties > Column**. Remove the vertical border on the outside if you want it to look like paper. Then go to **File > Save As** and pick **Word Template (.dotx)** so every new document opens from the Cornell layout.

**GoodNotes** includes Cornell paper among its built-in templates. In a notebook, open the **More** menu in the toolbar, choose **Change Template**, and pick a Cornell page in the size and color you want. In **Notability**, the most reliable route is to export the Word or Google Docs version above as a PDF and import it, or draw the two lines once with the ruler and copy that page for each new lecture.

sections.h2: What does a filled Cornell notes example look like?
sections.body: Here is a complete Cornell notes example from an introductory psychology lecture on memory and forgetting, the kind of class taught in PSY 101 at most US universities. Notice that the cues are questions, not headings. A heading like "Ebbinghaus" tells you what the note is about. A question like "What did Ebbinghaus find about forgetting?" makes you retrieve the answer.

headers: Notes: Intro to Psychology, Lecture 9, Memory and Forgetting
rows: Who first measured forgetting, and how?
Hermann Ebbinghaus, Über das Gedächtnis (On Memory), 1885. Memorized lists of nonsense syllables (e.g. DAX, BOK) and tested himself at intervals.
What does the forgetting curve show?
Steep drop in recall within the first hours and days, then the curve flattens. Most loss happens early.
What slows forgetting?
Spaced repetition: reviewing at growing intervals (1 day, 3 days, 1 week). Each review flattens the curve further.
Encoding vs storage vs retrieval?
Encoding = getting info in; storage = keeping it; retrieval = getting it out. Many 'memory problems' are retrieval failures.
What is the testing effect?
Roediger and Karpicke, 2006: students who tested themselves remembered more a week later than students who reread the same text.
Link to exam?
Prof hinted: compare spacing vs massed practice (cramming) in an essay question.
SUMMARY

Ebbinghaus showed that most forgetting happens soon after learning. Spaced review and self-testing slow it down, because they practise retrieval rather than re-exposure. This is why the Cornell cue column works: reciting from cues is a self-test.

callout.label: What makes this a good example
callout.body: The cues are written in the student's words, each one points to a single note, and the summary connects the lecture to how the student will study. A summary that only lists topics ("Ebbinghaus, spacing, testing effect") would not pass the Reflect step.

sections.h2: How do you make Cornell notes from a lecture transcript?
sections.body:
You make Cornell notes from a lecture transcript by treating the transcript as your Record step, then doing Reduce, Recite and Reflect yourself. This is a workflow, not an automatic feature: LessonScriptor transcribes the lecture in a Chrome side panel, and you move the important lines into your Cornell page afterwards. Nothing formats the page for you, and that is the point, because the Reduce step is where learning happens.

The workflow suits recorded lectures on Canvas, Moodle, Blackboard or Panopto, YouTube course videos, and live classes on Zoom or Google Meet in the browser.

steps.detail: Open the lecture in Chrome and start LessonScriptor in the side panel. Free mode uses your browser's speech engine through the microphone, so keep the speakers at about 80% volume and do not wear headphones. AI mode captures the tab audio directly, works with headphones, and handles accents and jargon better (30-minute free trial, then one-time packs from $5).

steps.strategy: Mark key lines as you listen
steps.detail: Instead of writing, highlight important sentences in the transcript (there are 5 highlight colors), bold definitions, and add a header when the lecturer changes topic. Take a screenshot of any slide you will need.
Export as .md (or .txt, or copy to clipboard) and open your Cornell template next to it.
Move only the highlighted lines into the notes column and shorten each one to a phrase. A 60-minute lecture produces thousands of words of transcript; your notes column should hold a page or two.
Write one question per note in the cue column, then the 3-4 sentence summary. Recite with the notes covered before you close the page.

callout.label: Why this fits students with ADHD
callout.body: Recording happens on its own, so your attention goes to the steps that actually build memory: choosing what matters, turning it into questions, and testing yourself. You are no longer splitting focus between listening and handwriting, which is the part of Cornell notes many ADHD students find hardest.

sections.h2: How can students with ADHD adapt Cornell notes?
sections.body: Students with ADHD can use Cornell notes, but the classic version asks for three things at once during class: listening, deciding what matters, and writing fast. Working memory is the bottleneck. These adjustments keep the structure and remove the overload.

subsections.body: Do not try to fill the notes column live. Let a transcript or the recording handle Record, and schedule Reduce as its own short session the same day.
Set a 25-minute timer and process one lecture section per block. A finished half-page beats an abandoned full page.

subsections.h3: Cap the summary at three sentences
subsections.body: A blank summary box invites perfectionism. Three sentences, one each for what, why and how it links, is enough to pass Reflect.

subsections.h3: Use color as the cue system
subsections.body: Give each color one job, for example yellow for definitions and blue for likely exam points, so scanning a page takes seconds instead of rereading it.

subsections.h3: Recite out loud or with someone
subsections.body: Answering cues out loud, or with a study partner over a call, keeps the Recite step from becoming silent rereading.

sections.h2: How do Cornell notes compare with other note-taking methods?
sections.body: Cornell notes are the best general-purpose method when you need to revise for exams, because the self-test is built in. Other methods win in specific situations.

rows: Cornell
Lectures you will be examined on; built-in self-testing
Needs a review session after class to be useful
Outline
Well-structured lectures with clear headings
No retrieval step; easy to just reread
Mind mapping
Seeing links between concepts, brainstorming essays
Hard to keep up with a fast lecturer
Charting
Comparing several items on the same criteria (theories, countries, drugs)
Only works when the content fits a grid
Sentence method
Fast lectures with little structure
Produces long, hard-to-review notes

summary.heading: The short version
summary.body: A Cornell notes template is a cue column, a notes column and a summary box, and the method behind it is Pauk's 5 Rs. Copy the template above into Docs, Notion, Word or GoodNotes, fill the cues after class rather than during it, and recite from them every week. If writing while listening is the step that breaks for you, let a transcript do the recording and keep your focus for the cues.

questions.question: Are Cornell notes good for ADHD?
questions.answer: Cornell notes are good for ADHD when you separate capture from processing. The cue column and summary give a clear structure and a built-in self-test. What usually fails is writing notes live while listening, so many ADHD students record or transcribe the lecture and fill the Cornell page afterwards in short, timed sessions.

questions.question: Cornell notes vs outline method: which is better?
questions.answer: The Cornell method is better for exam revision because the cue column turns your notes into a self-test. The outline method is faster to write and works well for clearly structured lectures, but it has no retrieval step. Many students outline in the notes column and add Cornell cues afterwards, which combines both.

questions.question: What are the 5 Rs of Cornell notes?
questions.answer: The 5 Rs of Cornell notes are Record, Reduce, Recite, Reflect and Review. You record notes during class, reduce them into cues and a summary after class, recite by answering cues with the notes covered, reflect on how the material connects, and review older pages weekly.

questions.question: How big should the columns be in a Cornell notes template?
questions.answer: On US Letter paper, the classic Cornell layout is a 2.5-inch cue column, a 6-inch notes column and a 2-inch summary at the bottom. On A4, use roughly 6 cm, 15 cm and 5 cm. Digitally, aim for about a 30/70 split between cues and notes.

questions.question: Is there a Cornell notes template in Google Docs?
questions.answer: Google Docs has no built-in Cornell template, but you can make one in five minutes with a 2 x 3 table: header row, cues and notes row, and a merged summary row. Save it as a master file and use File > Make a copy for each lecture.

questions.question: Can I make Cornell notes from a lecture transcript?
questions.answer: Yes. Use the transcript as your Record step: transcribe the lecture with a tool such as LessonScriptor, highlight the key lines, export them as .md, then move the highlights into the notes column and write the cues and summary yourself. The tool does not create the Cornell page for you.

questions.question: Who invented Cornell notes?
questions.answer: Walter Pauk invented Cornell notes in the 1950s while directing the Reading and Study Center at Cornell University. He published the system in How to Study in College, first released in 1962.
